claims.text: The starting material is additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an FCC matrix.
The as-built microstructure contains residual stresses and minor surface oxidation typical of additive manufacturing.
Catastrophic failure during high-temperature exposure is governed by formation and coarsening of brittle grain-boundary oxides.
In oxidizing environments, Al, Cr, and Ti preferentially oxidize at grain boundaries.
Preferential grain-boundary oxidation forms a continuous, embrittling oxide network.
A continuous grain-boundary oxide network undermines intergranular cohesion.
Grain-boundary oxide formation depletes key alloying elements near the boundaries.
Rapid oxygen diffusion at elevated temperature drives preferential oxidation of Al, Cr, and Ti at grain boundaries.
Loss of grain-boundary cohesion facilitates crack initiation and rapid intergranular crack propagation.
Rapid intergranular crack propagation leads to catastrophic failure.
Mildly reducing conditions suppress continuous external oxide-scale formation.
Under reducing conditions, localized or dispersed internal oxidation occurs and destabilizes the phase structure.
Higher oxygen partial pressure will produce thicker and more contiguous grain-boundary oxide layers than the as-built baseline and mildly reducing exposure.
Higher oxygen partial pressure will produce more pronounced depletion of Al, Cr, and Ti near grain boundaries.
The thicker, more continuous oxide network will reduce fracture toughness and cause earlier catastrophic failure under thermal cycling or mechanical loading.
Mildly reducing exposure will produce less continuous oxide films but observable internal oxidation and potentially different failure modes.
The proposed mechanism applies over 700–900 °C and exposure durations from hours to tens of hours, where diffusion-driven oxidation is significant.
The proposed mechanism may cease to govern when oxidation kinetics are minimal or when rapid thermal cycling or other mechanisms dominate.
